subsystems.name: Science instruments
subsystems.role: identify organic molecules, salts and gases in plume material.

subsystems.name: Sample collection system
subsystems.role: capture ice grains and vapour without destroying their chemistry.
parts: aerogel or low-density collector for flyby
scoop or drill for surface fallout on a lander

subsystems.name: Spacecraft bus
subsystems.role: carry and operate the payload for years in deep space.

subsystems.name: Navigation and guidance
subsystems.role: steer the craft through a narrow plume at kilometres per second.

subsystems.name: Sample return stage (optional)
subsystems.role: bring collected material back to Earth without contamination.

subsystems.name: Planetary protection system
subsystems.role: keep Earth microbes out and, on return, alien material in.

buildSteps.title: Choose the target vent
buildSteps.detail: Use Cassini data and new orbital reconnaissance to pick a plume vent that is active, rich in organics and reachable at a safe flyby altitude.

buildSteps.title: Design the trajectory
buildSteps.detail: Plan gravity assists past Venus, Earth and Jupiter to reach Saturn, then either a series of Enceladus flybys or orbit insertion followed by a landing.

buildSteps.title: Prove the collector
buildSteps.detail: Fire ice grains at kilometres per second into candidate collector materials in a vacuum chamber to show they survive intact for analysis.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the spacecraft
buildSteps.detail: Integrate instruments, power source, communications and thermal control in a cleanroom, with sterilisation for the parts that touch the plume.

buildSteps.title: Launch and cruise
buildSteps.detail: Launch on a heavy rocket and spend roughly seven to ten years cruising to Saturn, keeping instruments and samples cold and uncontaminated.

buildSteps.title: Arrive and approach
buildSteps.detail: Perform Saturn orbit insertion, then a series of Enceladus flybys to map the plumes and select the exact encounter geometry.

buildSteps.title: Sample the plume
buildSteps.detail: Fly through the plume at high speed with the collector open, or land near a vent and collect fresh fallout from the surface.

buildSteps.title: Analyse or return
buildSteps.detail: Either analyse the material in situ with mass spectrometry and radio the results home, or seal it and launch it back to Earth for study in laboratories.

prerequisites.why: solar power at Saturn needs impractically large panels, so a nuclear source is needed to run instruments and keep samples cold.
Stardust captured comet dust at about 6 km/s, but Enceladus plume encounters are faster and the ice is more fragile.
Cassini's instruments detected organics and molecular hydrogen, but a life-detection mission needs far greater sensitivity and selectivity.
comet missions have navigated close to small bodies, but threading a narrow plume at kilometres per second demands tighter autonomy.
no sample has been returned from an ocean world, and protocols for sealing and curating possibly habitable material are not yet proven.
Stardust and Hayabusa returned small samples, providing a basis for a sealed capsule and dedicated curation facility.

pathway.milestone: Cassini (2004–2017) discovered the plumes and found salts, silica, organics and molecular hydrogen in them
pathway.unlocks: evidence that Enceladus has a subsurface ocean with hydrothermal activity and the chemical ingredients for life.

pathway.milestone: a dedicated orbiter or lander such as the Enceladus Orbilander concept to characterise the plume and ocean habitability
pathway.unlocks: detailed maps of vents, plume composition over time, and a proven design for sampling.

pathway.milestone: a plume sample return mission that brings ice grains and vapour back to Earth
pathway.unlocks: definitive laboratory analysis for biosignatures that no spacecraft instrument can match.

pathway.milestone: subsurface access or a landed laboratory on Enceladus
pathway.unlocks: direct study of the ocean and its chemistry, independent of what the plumes happen to carry.
